source.title: The Impact of Neural Network Overparameterization on Gradient Confusion and Stochastic Gradient Descent
source.authors: Karthik Abinav Sankararaman; Soham De; Zheng Xu; W. R. Huang; T. Goldstein

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendix, is present. Some plots are flattened into the text and do not provide recoverable numerical values.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures training loss and gradient confusion while varying depth, skip connections, and batch normalization, bearing on V3's trainability claim; it does not measure classification error.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-loss and gradient-confusion results for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. It does not report training classification error, so these results do not test V1's zero-error claim. The width sweeps and MNIST depth/width experiments do not measure a version's named outcome. Values for the selected CIFAR-10 depth and shortcut/normalization comparisons are shown only in figures.
record.test_reason: The study reports training loss and gradient confusion, rather than V3's training classification error or V6's accuracy gain over time and learning-rate tolerance. Its width experiments do not measure V2's spurious minima in teacher-student problems. Its initialization theorem concerns gradient confusion in linear networks, without measuring V4's learning speed or trainable depth. These are related findings, but they do not directly test the versions as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors conclude that greater width lowers gradient confusion and improves SGD trainability under standard Gaussian initialization, whereas greater depth has the opposite tendency. Combining batch normalization with skip connections improves deep-model training. Their orthogonal-initialization result for linear networks suggests a possible route to improving very deep networks.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments vary architecture and measure training loss and gradient confusion rather than directly measuring the claim's training classification error. They use SGD on CIFAR image classification tasks.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth, width, batch normalization, and skip connections change the reported training-loss and gradient-confusion outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report slower convergence and worse final training loss as CNN depth increases. Batch normalization or skip connections individually help, while their combination improves deep-network trainability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested SGD recipes on CIFAR datasets, depth worsens training-loss optimization, and combining batch normalization with skip connections alleviates this difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: Width sweeps generally show faster training-loss convergence and lower gradient confusion; these experiments do not identify spurious local minima or use teacher-student models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing width can improve SGD training-loss convergence in the tested CNNs, residual networks, and MLPs.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 6.1 gives a depth-independent gradient-confusion bound for orthogonal linear networks with a depth-dependent output scaling and spherical random inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the theorem's assumptions, orthogonal linear networks have a gradient-confusion bound independent of depth.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The relevant numerical training-loss values are only in figures and cannot be recovered from the supplied text. The experiments report loss rather than training classification error. Runs unable to decrease loss were ignored; at least 4 of 5 runs completed. No results test random or corrupted labels.
record.rows_left_out: Width sweeps and additional CNN, WRN, CIFAR-100, and MNIST results were not extracted because they measure training loss or gradient confusion without testing a version's named outcome beyond the selected V3 depth and shortcut/normalization results. Relevant plots include Figures 2–3, 5–15 and Appendix A.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error, including corrupted or random labels and the specified model-size and training-recipe comparisons.
Spurious local minima and the effect of one or two additional student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Depth degradation in training classification error and its prevention by identity shortcuts; longer-training controls; the special tanh initialization and Fixup clauses.
Initialization-dependent learning speed and trainable depth, including orthogonal versus Gaussian tanh training and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Loss recovery above the initial stability limit, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence relative to the threshold.
Accuracy gain over training time, tolerance of higher learning rates with batch normalization, and Fixup comparisons without normalization.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 4 includes depths 52, 76, and 100 as well as the five depths extracted. The record declares additional plots omitted, so these are not undeclared missing results. All figure values remain unreadable in the supplied text. Learning rates were tuned separately for each model using average final training loss; unsuccessful runs were excluded, with at least four of five runs completing. The resulting comparisons do not estimate unconditional training success rates. No listed original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and comparisons with smaller models or early stopping.
Two-layer teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.

ImageNet; training classification error; longer training as a separate condition; plain batch-normalized networks compared directly with residual networks under identical settings beyond the reported CIFAR-10 loss plots.
Whether initialization choices themselves change training speed or trainable depth, including orthogonal versus Gaussian training comparisons and 10,000-layer networks.
Learning rates above the stability limit, curvature or sharpness behavior, and divergence thresholds.
Accuracy gain over training time, tolerance of higher learning rates, and Fixup without normalization.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The study discusses the claimed optimization findings while investigating related measures; it does not directly test a listed version or use its finding solely as a tool.

tranche.reason: The results measure training loss and gradient confusion, without establishing the versions' training classification error, teacher-student spurious minima, initialization-dependent learning speed, stability-threshold recovery, or batch-normalization accuracy speed and learning-rate tolerance. The orthogonal-initialization theorem bounds gradient confusion in linear networks.

source_check.notes: Figure 4 confirms all listed depths and normalization/shortcut conditions; individual loss values are unavailable in the flattened text, correctly retained as figure only. Appendix A.2 excludes runs that failed to decrease loss and selects learning rates by mean final training loss.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR-10 CNNs with batch normalization and skip connections across the tested depth sweep
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that the combined techniques keep gradient confusion relatively low and significantly improve deep-model trainability; Figure 4(a) shows the corresponding training-loss series (R16–R20).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR-10 CNNs with either batch normalization alone or skip connections alone
reader_labels.reason: Each technique helps individually, but the paper says these models still worsen as depth increases (R6–R15).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR-10 CNNs without batch normalization or skip connections across the tested depth sweep
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports increasing depth slows convergence and increases gradient confusion; Figure 4(a) plots training loss for depths 16 through 40 (R1–R5).
